question: The fight against corruption requires specialised, independent anti-corruption institutions and courageous officials backed by the law and state institutions. They must have certainty that the prosecution of even the highest-ranking officials and politicians will be met with genuine state support, rather than reprisals.

Unfortunately, the return to power of parties tainted by corruption scandals is often accompanied by vindictiveness, the stalling of investigations and the persecution of those who had the courage to tackle corruption at the highest levels.

This is what has happened following the return to power of the Civic Platform, a party which has been implicated in numerous corruption scandals throughout its history, and whose leader is a politician known for his extreme vindictiveness towards those who expose corruption within his inner circle.

A prime example of Poland’s efforts in the fight against corruption is the case of Sławomir Nowak, Tusk’s chief of staff and Minister for Infrastructure, who was charged with over a dozen corruption offences. Following the change of government, the so-called ‘Polish plot’ case was discontinued, even though the evidence gathered during the investigation was not considered during the trial1.

Instead, the disciplinary officer took action against the prosecutor who drafted the indictment, Jan Drelewski, and Minister Żurek issued a decree dismissing him from the special anti-corruption unit, despite the unequivocal opposition of the prosecutor in charge of that division2. 1.
As it draws up its anti-corruption strategy, is the Commission analysing examples of high-level corruption? Is the Commission familiar with the corruption case involving Sławomir Nowak?

In its strategy, will the Commission pay due attention to protecting public officials, whose courage enables the exposure and prosecution of corruption at the highest levels of government, from reprisals?

The decision prompted a wave of criticism, as the prosecution withdrew the charges against Nowak five years after the indictment had been filed and after three and a half years of the case ‘gathering dust’ in the District Court.

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) Strengthening the rule of law and combating corruption are key priorities for the Commission. This is reflected, in particular, in its commitment to adopt an EU Anti-Corruption Strategy1. The Strategy will set out an overarching and comprehensive EU approach to prevent and fight corruption effectively.

When it comes to individual cases or specific criminal investigations, Member States are solely responsible for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security. The Commission monitors and reports on developments regarding the fight against corruption in all Member States, including Poland, as part of the annual Rule of Law Report.
Where needed, the report also includes concrete recommendations aimed at strengthening anticorruption frameworks2.
